Neural network quantum states in the grand canonical ensemble

Anton Hul Email: a.hul@uw.edu.pl Affiliation: Faculty of Physics, University of Warsaw, 02-093 Warsaw, Poland    Matija Medvidović Email: mmedvidovic@ethz.ch Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zürich, 8093 Zürich, Switzerland    Juan Carrasquilla Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zürich, 8093 Zürich, Switzerland
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Variational Monte Carlo calculations have recently reached state-of-the-art accuracy in the approximation of ground state properties of quantum many-body systems. Making use of flexible neural quantum states and automatic differentiation has bypassed traditional computational obstacles such as reliance on basis sets. In this paper, we propose a neural quantum state architecture capable of representing symmetric bosonic wavefunctions in Fock space, enabling the study of systems with variable particle number. By supplementing our variational state with Monte Carlo sampling and geometric optimization, we demonstrate competitive variational energies across an array of one- and two-dimensional systems, converging to the physical boson number under a set chemical potential. Our approach enables accurate estimates of one-body reduced density matrices, opening access to observables such as condensate fractions and radial density profiles from first principles. Our method opens the door to numerical predictions of key measurable quantities in practical grand canonical systems.

I Introduction

A fundamental challenge in the classical simulation of quantum many-body systems stems from the computational complexity associated with the storage and manipulation of an exact representation of the quantum state, which scale exponentially with the number of particles in the system. This observation has motivated the development of a wide array of algorithms and efficient compression strategies for quantum many-body states with an eye on solving currently intractable problems in strongly correlated quantum matter [1]. In recent years, neural quantum states (NQS) [14, 13, 12, 19] have emerged, offering a favorable tradeoff between expressive power and computational efficiency. Motivated by explosive progress within the field of artificial intelligence (AI), recent breakthroughs in variational Monte Carlo (VMC) have leveraged massively parallel modern hardware and algorithms to bypass traditional computational bottlenecks [42, 37].

A key example of such a computational upgrade is performing calculations directly in first quantization. Removing the reliance on basis sets, modern variational calculations have reached unprecedented accuracy [63] in difficult many-fermion calculations in quantum chemistry [51, 27, 62, 22, 28], electron gas systems [49, 32, 55, 39], nuclear physics [40], and even non-equilibrium dynamics [46, 54]. Rapid algorithmic advances continue to unlock new physical insights for quantum physics at scale.

Traditional approaches assume a fixed number of particles NN. However, the chemical potential μ\mu may induce phase transitions, control density fluctuations, and determine the thermodynamic stability for systems amenable to a description in terms of the grand canonical ensemble (GCE). Recent experiments with cold atoms [36], photonic condensates in optical microcavities [53] or exciton-polariton condensates [10] display natural grand canonical statistics. The violation of particle number conservation in these systems makes them unsuitable for study using the canonical NQS-VMC pipeline.

Bosonic quantum field theories are a key research frontier for variational methods. First-quantized variational calculations on bosonic systems in Refs. [48, 4, 24] report accurate results, testing predictions for prototypical bosonic models. A field-theoretic description has been proposed by Ref. [41] and has demonstrated accuracy in one-dimensional systems, with a full treatment of particle number fluctuations in the grand canonical formalism.

Discrete Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians successfully describe deep optical lattices. However, they fundamentally fail to capture the physics of continuous 1D systems and shallow traps. Experimental observations of a one-dimensional Tonks-Girardeau gas [34] and the quantum Newton’s cradle [35] have highlighted the rich correlated dynamics in the continuum. Modeling these systems from first principles necessitates flexible, continuous-space variational architectures capable of handling particle fluctuations in the grand canonical ensemble.

In this paper, we propose a form for the total variational wavefunction in Fock space. Exploiting the natural permutation equivariance of the transformer architecture [59, 21, 62, 57, 61], we construct a symmetric and systematically improvable trial state. Due to the transformer masking mechanism, our state is capable of outputting amplitudes from many particle-number sectors using the same set of variational parameters. All our calculations are performed by sampling configurations directly in coordinate space, avoiding biases associated with single-particle basis sets.

Additionally, we propose a method to efficiently compute grand canonical one-body reduced density matrices, yielding precise numerical estimates of experimentally measurable observables, such as condensate fractions and single-particle densities. Crucially, our approach converges to an integer number of particles under a set chemical potential for particle-conserving Hamiltonians, revealing ensemble equivalence without unnecessary assumptions.

Our grand canonical variational quantum field state is tested against an array of bosonic Hamiltonians in one and two dimensions. The Lieb-Liniger [38] and Calogero-Sutherland [11, 58, 44, 31] models are used as accuracy benchmarks, where we show precise agreement with exact results. We treat harmonically trapped bosons with short-range interactions as well, extracting accurate variational wavefunctions and demonstrating the practical applicability of modern VMC to real-world systems.

II Methods

II.1 Models

Consider a general number-conserving Hamiltonian in the GCE, H=H1+H2H=H_{1}+H_{2} with:

H1=∫ℝdd𝐫​ψ^†​(𝐫)​(−∇22​m+V⁡(𝐫)−μ)​ψ^​(𝐫)H2=12​∫ℝdd𝐫​d𝐫′​W​(𝐫,𝐫′)​ψ^†​(𝐫)​ψ^†​(𝐫′)​ψ​(𝐫′)​ψ​(𝐫),\begin{gathered}H_{1}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\differential{\rr}\,\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\left(-\frac{\nabla^{2}}{2m}+V({\mathbf{r}})-\mu\right)\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}})\\ H_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\differential{\rr}\differential{\rr'}\,W({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\psi({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\psi({\mathbf{r}})\;,\end{gathered} (1)

formulated as a dd-dimensional spatial integral over one- and two-body terms, respectively. The Hamiltonian is expressed within the framework of second quantization, where the fields are represented by the creation and annihilation operators ψ^†​(𝐫)\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}}) and ψ^​(𝐫)\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}}). It comprises the kinetic energy term, an external potential V⁡(𝐫)V({\mathbf{r}}), and a two-body interaction potential W⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)W({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}). The particle number is not fixed but is instead determined by the chemical potential μ\mu.

In this framework, the quantum field states live in Fock space and can be expressed as a superposition of nn-particle wave functions:

|Ψ⟩=⨁n=0∞∫ℝd​nd𝐑n​ϕn​(𝐑n)​|𝐑n⟩.|\Psi\rangle=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{dn}}\differential{\rR_n}\,\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})\,|{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rangle\,. (2)

As required in bosonic quantum field theories, the functions are permutation-invariant, unnormalized, and can be obtained by projecting the field state onto the corresponding basis state, ϕn​(𝐑n)=⟨𝐑n|Ψ⟩\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|\Psi\rangle.

II.2 Variational ansatz

The variational ansatz is used to parametrize each nn-particle wave function ϕn​(𝐑n)\phi_{n}(\mathbf{R}_{n}) using a common neural network architecture. The architecture should be capable of handling an arbitrary or sufficiently large number of input arguments, i.e., particle positions, since the number of particles is not fixed.

The originally proposed ansatz for representing ϕn​(𝐑n)\phi_{n}(\mathbf{R}_{n}) in one-dimensional systems relied on the Deep Sets (DS) neural network architecture [41], which is permutation-invariant and naturally suited for inputs of variable size.

In this work, we propose an alternative neural network ansatz based on the well-known transformer (TF) architecture [59]. As shown in Fig. 2, the ansatz consists of LL identical transformer blocks. Each block includes a masked multi-head self-attention (MHA) layer with HH heads, preceded by layer normalization [2], and followed by a postprocessing sub-layer composed of layer normalization, linear layers, and activation functions.

For a given input configuration 𝐑n∈ℝn×d{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}, the MHA mechanism constructs three sets of matrices for each attention head hh:

  • •

    the queries Q(h)=𝐑n​WQ(h)∈ℝn×dkQ^{(h)}={\mathbf{R}}_{n}W_{Q}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{k}},

  • •

    the keys K(h)=𝐑n​WK(h)∈ℝn×dkK^{(h)}={\mathbf{R}}_{n}W_{K}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{k}},

  • •

    the values V(h)=𝐑n​WV(h)∈ℝn×dvV^{(h)}={\mathbf{R}}_{n}W_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{v}},

where WQ(h)W_{Q}^{(h)}, WK(h)∈ℝd×dkW_{K}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{k}}, and WV(h)∈ℝd×dvW_{V}^{(h)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{v}} are trainable projection matrices.

Given a mask M∈ℝn×nM\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} encoding the absence of particles at each input position, the attention weights for head hh are computed as

A(h)=softmax⁡(Q(h)​K(h)⊤+Mdk)∈ℝn×n,A^{(h)}=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q^{(h)}{K^{(h)}}^{\top}+M}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, (3)

where the softmax is applied row-wise. The weighted combination of values, A(h)​V(h)A^{(h)}V^{(h)}, from all HH heads is then concatenated and projected back to the original feature dimension. The weights of the attention matrices and linear layers are shared across all particles, but are optimized independently for each transformer block.

Given a permutation matrix P∈ℝn×nP\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} acting on the particle indices, the permuted input configuration is P​𝐑nP{\mathbf{R}}_{n}. The queries and keys transform as

Q(h)​K(h)⊤↦(P​Q(h))​(P​K(h))⊤=P​Q(h)​K(h)⊤​P⊤.Q^{(h)}{K^{(h)}}^{\top}\;\mapsto\;(PQ^{(h)})(PK^{(h)})^{\top}=P\,Q^{(h)}{K^{(h)}}^{\top}P^{\top}. (4)

After applying the row-wise softmax, the attention matrix satisfies A(h)↦P​A(h)​P⊤A^{(h)}\;\mapsto\;PA^{(h)}P^{\top}. Consequently, the value aggregation transforms as

A(h)​V(h)↦(P​A(h)​P⊤)​(P​V(h))=P⁡(A(h)​V(h)).A^{(h)}V^{(h)}\;\mapsto\;(PA^{(h)}P^{\top})(PV^{(h)})=P\bigl(A^{(h)}V^{(h)}\bigr). (5)

By construction, the MHA mechanism guarantees permutation equivariance of the output with respect to the particle positions 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n}. We then apply a LogSumExp pooling operator to obtain a permutation-invariant global representation:

LogSumExp​(x)=log⁡(∑i=1kai​exi).\text{LogSumExp}(x)=\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}e^{x_{i}}\right). (6)

A detailed specification of the trainable parameters, including the number of attention heads, transformer layers, and typical embedding dimensions, is provided in Appendix A.

In systems with closed boundary conditions, the single-particle coordinates 𝐫i∈ℝd{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are embedded into a higher kk-dimensional space using physically motivated Gaussian functions:

𝐫i⟶exp⁡(−|Δ​𝐫i|22​σ2)∈ℝmd,{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\;\longrightarrow\;\exp\!\left(-\frac{|\Delta{\mathbf{r}}_{i}|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{d}}, (7)

where mm denotes the number of uniformly spaced grid points along each of the dd physical dimensions, and Δ​𝐫i=|𝐫i−𝐬|\Delta\mathbf{r}_{i}=|{\mathbf{r}}_{i}-\mathbf{s}| is the distance between the single-particle coordinate and the grid point 𝐬\mathbf{s}. The parameter σ\sigma, which determines the width of the Gaussian functions, is kept constant and is chosen such that each Gaussian spans several grid points. The resulting dd-dimensional grid representation is subsequently flattened into a one-dimensional array of length k=mdk=m^{d}.

In the presence of periodic boundary conditions (PBCs), the coordinates are embedded into a truncated LL-periodic Fourier basis [48]:

𝐫i⟶[sin⁡(2​π​jL​𝐫i),cos⁡(2​π​jL​𝐫i)]j=1m∈ℝ2​m​d.{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\;\longrightarrow\;\left[\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi j}{L}{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\right),\;\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi j}{L}{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\right)\right]_{j=1}^{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{2md}. (8)

where sin⁡(𝐫i)\sin(\rr_i) and cos⁡(𝐫i)\cos(\rr_i) denote the component-wise application of the trigonometric functions to the vector 𝐫i{\mathbf{r}}_{i}. The resulting representation is flattened into a one-dimensional array of length k=2​m​dk=2md.

The final nn-particle wave function φn​(𝐑n)\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) is obtained by multiplying the ansatz output φ~n​(𝐑n)\tilde{\varphi}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) by additional factors introduced to enhance convergence during optimization. These may include a cutoff factor, which enforces the vanishing of the wave function at the system boundaries in closed systems, or a Jastrow factor, which ensures the correct short-range behavior of the wave function (see Appendix B for further details).

II.3 Variational Monte Carlo

The standard VMC approach enables the estimation of expectation values of a generic quantum mechanical operator QQ of the form

⟨Q⟩=⟨ψθ|Q|ψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩\langle Q\rangle=\frac{\langle\psi_{\theta}|Q|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle} (9)

where |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle is a variational many-body state defined by amplitudes ψθ​(𝐱)\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) in a basis 𝐱\mathbf{x}. The direct calculation of expectation values in the numerator and denominator is generally intractable. However, they can be estimated efficiently via Monte Carlo integration.

An unbiased estimator for the expectation value in Eq. (9) can be obtained as the empirical mean of Qnloc​(𝐱)Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}(\mathbf{x}) over NsN_{s} configurations 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} sampled from |φ¯​(𝐱)|2|\bar{\varphi}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}:

⟨Q⟩=𝔼𝐱∼|φ¯​(𝐱)|2​[Qnloc​(𝐱)]≈1Ns​∑i=1NsQnloc​(𝐱i),\langle Q\rangle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim|\bar{\varphi}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}}\bigl[Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}(\mathbf{x})\bigr]\approx\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}(\mathbf{x}_{i}), (10)

where the local observable Qnloc​(𝐱)Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}(\mathbf{x}) is defined as

Qnloc​(𝐱)=⟨𝐱|Q|ψθ⟩⟨𝐱|ψθ⟩,Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\langle\mathbf{x}|Q|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{x}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}, (11)

and the normalized probability density is

|φ¯​(𝐱)|2=|ψθ​(𝐱)|2∫d​𝐱′​|ψθ​(𝐱′)|2.|\bar{\varphi}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}=\frac{|\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}}{\int d\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\,|\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})|^{2}}. (12)

An analogous method for estimating observables in the context of QFTs was developed in Ref. [41]. The approach, referred to as VMC in Fock space, expresses the expectation value of an nn-particle local observable function Qnloc​(𝐑n)Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) for a quantum field state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle, as

⟨Q⟩=⟨Ψ|Q|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=𝔼n∼Pn𝔼𝐑n∼|φ¯n|2[Qnloc(𝐑n)],\langle Q\rangle=\frac{\langle\Psi|Q|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}=\EX_{n\sim P_{n}}\EX_{{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\biggr[Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})\biggr]\,, (13)

where the n-particle local observable of the configuration 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} is

Qnloc​(𝐑n)=⟨𝐑n|Q|Ψ⟩⟨𝐑n|Ψ⟩Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\frac{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|Q|\Psi\rangle}{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|\Psi\rangle} (14)

with the probability distribution of the particle number

Pn=⟨φn|φn⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=∫dn​𝐫​|φn​(𝐑n)|2∑m=0∞∫dn​𝐫′​|φm​(𝐑m′)|2P_{n}=\frac{\langle\varphi_{n}|\varphi_{n}\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}=\frac{\int d^{n}{\mathbf{r}}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}{\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\int d^{n}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}|\varphi_{m}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{m})|^{2}} (15)

and the probability distribution of the n-particle wave function

|φ¯n​(𝐑n)|2=|φn​(𝐑n)|2∫dn​𝐫′​|φn​(𝐑n′)|2.|\bar{\varphi}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}=\frac{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}{\int d^{n}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{n})|^{2}}\,. (16)

The approach can be seen as a natural generalization of the traditional VMC, where the expectation value is extended to include both the distribution of the nn-particle wave function and the particle number distribution.

II.4 Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling

To obtain the samples {𝐑i:i=1,…,Ns}\{{\mathbf{R}}_{i}:i=1,\dots,N_{s}\} necessary for estimating observables in Eq. (13), it is common practice to employ well-established Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers. In this work, we largely follow the sampling procedure outlined in Ref. [41].

As in standard MCMC algorithms, the procedure in Fock space begins by proposing a new configuration 𝐑n′{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime} from the current configuration 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n}, which is then accepted or rejected according to the Metropolis–Hastings rule. In our scheme, new bosonic configurations 𝐑n′{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime} are proposed while also allowing the particle number nn to change. With probability 2​p±2p_{\pm}, the particle number is either increased or decreased, each occurring with probability p±p_{\pm}. With probability p0=1−2​p±p_{0}=1-2p_{\pm}, the proposed configuration preserves the particle number, and a uniform random displacement is applied to all particle positions:

𝐑n→𝐑n′=𝐑n+𝜻,{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime}={\mathbf{R}}_{n}+\bm{\zeta}, (17)

where 𝜻∼U⁡([−w2,w2]d)\bm{\zeta}\sim U\left([-\tfrac{w}{2},\tfrac{w}{2}]^{d}\right) is a dd-dimensional uniform random vector of width ww.

The probabilities of individual configurations 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n}, as well as the transition probabilities 𝐑n→𝐑n′{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime}, are given in detail in Appendix E. In practice, we run multiple MCMC chains in parallel, and estimate expectation values as empirical means over all collected samples 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} with different particle numbers nn. The uncertainty of the estimated expectation value is computed as the standard deviation of the corresponding means across the chains.

II.5 Stochastic optimization

The goal of VMC is to minimize the energy expectation value with respect to the trial state |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle by finding the optimal variational parameters

θopt=argminθE​(θ)=argminθ⟨ψθ|H|ψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩≥E0,\theta_{\text{opt}}=\argmin_{\theta}E(\theta)=\argmin_{\theta}\frac{\langle\psi_{\theta}|H|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}\geq E_{0}\,, (18)

where E0E_{0} is the true ground state energy. Standard gradient-based optimization methods can be employed to determine the optimal parameters θopt\theta_{\text{opt}} by iteratively updating the parameters using the energy gradient with respect to the variational parameters g=∇θE​(θ)g=\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta), starting from an initial guess.

A more general optimization strategy, motivated by physical principles and based on imaginary-time evolution, is known as natural gradient descent (NG) or stochastic reconfiguration (SR) [56]. Within this framework, the updated ansatz parameters θ′\theta^{\prime} are obtained as

θ′=θ−η​S−1​g,\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\eta S^{-1}g, (19)

where η\eta denotes the learning rate, and SS is the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), also referred to as the quantum Fisher information matrix. The gradient and the QGT are given by [42]:

Sμ​ν=2Re{⟨Oμ†(Oν−⟨Oν⟩)⟩},gμ=2Re{⟨Oμ†(E−⟨E⟩)⟩},\begin{gathered}S_{\mu\nu}=2\real\left\{\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}(O_{\nu}-\langle O_{\nu}\rangle)\rangle\right\}\;,\\ g_{\mu}=2\real\left\{\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}(E-\langle E\rangle)\rangle\right\},\end{gathered} (20)

where the indices μ\mu and ν\nu run over the NpN_{p} variational parameters. The expectation values ⟨⋅⟩≡⟨ψθ|⋅|ψθ⟩/⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩\langle\cdot\rangle\equiv\langle\psi_{\theta}|\cdot|\psi_{\theta}\rangle/\langle\psi_{\theta}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle are taken with respect to the trial state |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle. The diagonal operators OμO_{\mu} are defined as

Oμ​|ψθ⟩=∂θμ|ψθ⟩.O_{\mu}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle=\partial_{\theta^{\mu}}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle\,. (21)

The gradient and QGT in Eq. (20) depend only on the local energy Enloc​(𝐑n)E^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) and the local operator Oνloc​(𝐑n)O^{\text{loc}}_{\nu}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}), which are sampled using the MCMC method described in Sec. II.4. This procedure enables efficient estimation of the gradient and QGT required for parameter optimization, without the need for direct evaluation of ∇θE​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta). Moreover, by applying the Woodbury identity, the effective matrix dimension for inversion can be reduced from Np×NpN_{p}\times N_{p} to Ns×NsN_{s}\times N_{s} [15]. Instead of performing an explicit matrix inversion, the corresponding system of linear equations is solved using a standard dense linear algebra solver.

III Results

In this section, we first compare the performance of the introduced TF ansatz with the originally developed DS ansatz. In Secs. III.1 and III.2.1, both architectures are applied to the exactly solvable one-dimensional Lieb–Liniger and Calogero–Sutherland models, respectively. We then focus exclusively on the TF ansatz in two-dimensional systems, studying the exactly solvable two-dimensional Calogero–Sutherland model in Sec. III.2.2. Finally, in Sec. III.3, we apply the TF ansatz to a system of harmonically confined bosons with Gaussian interactions. We show that our ansatz successfully reproduces the results obtained by exact diagonalization (ED) for a small number of bosons and, finally, present the results for an analytically unsolvable model in the grand-canonical ensemble.

III.1 Lieb-Liniger model

The original Lieb-Liniger model assumes the absence of an external potential V⁡(x)V(x) and describes an ensemble of NN bosons in a one-dimensional box of length LL, interacting via a repulsive two-body contact potential:

WLL​(x,y)=2​g​δ​(x−y),W_{\rm LL}(x,y)=2g\,\delta(x-y), (22)

with interaction strength g>0g>0. This model serves as a valuable numerical benchmark, allowing us to verify that both the DS and TF architectures can learn the ground state of a one-dimensional inhomogeneous system with short-range interactions and hard-wall boundaries, as well as to compare their performance.

We set the particle mass m=1m=1 and the box length L=1L=1, and first consider the Tonks-Girardeau (TG) limit, in which the interaction strength is g→∞g\to\infty. We also examine the performance of both architectures at a smaller interaction strength of g=10g=10. The comparison of the ground-state energies and particle numbers obtained from the converged ansatzes is presented in Table 1, together with the corresponding exact values for two regimes.

For a fair comparison, both models were configured with the same number of trainable parameters. While both architectures successfully converge to the correct ground-state energy, the TF architecture shows faster and smoother convergence and ultimately achieves a lower energy than the DS model. Moreover, the rescaled variance metric σ~E2\tilde{\sigma}^{2}_{E}, which is known to correlate with the accuracy of the wave function (see Appendix G), is one to two orders of magnitude smaller for the TF architecture.

To further verify the learned ground states, we calculate the particle number density, defined as:

n⁡(x)=⟨Ψ|​ψ^†​(x)​ψ^​(x)​|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩.n(x)=\frac{\bra{\Psi}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}(x)\hat{\psi}(x)\ket{\Psi}}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}. (23)

As shown in Fig. 3, the densities estimated using VMC sampling (see Appendix F) from the converged ansatzes perfectly match the exact analytical results.

III.2 Calogero-Sutherland model

III.2.1 One-dimensional case

Another valuable numerical benchmark for assessing whether both the DS and TF architectures can learn the ground state of a one-dimensional system with long-range interactions and periodic boundary conditions is the Calogero–Sutherland model. The model describes particles confined on a ring of circumference LL, interacting via a two-body periodic potential that decays as the inverse square of the distance between particles:

WCS​(x,y)=g​π2L2​[sin⁡(πL​(x−y))]−2W_{\rm CS}(x,y)=g\frac{\pi^{2}}{L^{2}}\left[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{L}(x-y)\right)\right]^{-2} (24)

Following the setup from Ref. [41], we set the system size L=5L=5 and study both weaker and stronger coupling regimes. The comparison of the ground-state energies and particle numbers obtained from the converged ansatzes together with the corresponding exact values for two regimes is presented in Table 2. The TF architecture once again yields a rescaled variance metric σ~E2\tilde{\sigma}^{2}_{E} that is an order of magnitude smaller.

Another observable that can be calculated is the ground-state one-body density matrix (OBDM), defined as:

ρ⁡(x,x′)=⟨Ψ|​ψ^†​(x′)​ψ^​(x)​|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩.\rho(x,x^{\prime})=\frac{\bra{\Psi}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}(x^{\prime})\hat{\psi}(x)\ket{\Psi}}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}. (25)

For the considered translation-invariant system, the OBDM depends only on the relative displacement, ρ⁡(s=|x−x′|)\rho(s=|x-x^{\prime}|). The resulting OBDMs estimated using VMC sampling (see Appendix F) from the converged ansatzes are shown in Fig. 4 and are in good agreement with the exact analytical results.

III.2.2 Two-dimensional case

An analytical extension of the original one-dimensional Calogero–Sutherland model to two dimensions is presented in Ref. [31]. The corresponding Hamiltonian describes a system of NN bosons confined within an isotropic harmonic potential,

V⁡(𝐫)=ω2​𝐫2,V({\mathbf{r}})=\omega^{2}{\mathbf{r}}^{2}, (26)

and interacting through an inverse-square two-body potential,

WCS(2)​(𝐫,𝐫′)=g|𝐫−𝐫′|2,W^{(2)}_{\rm CS}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\frac{g}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|^{2}}, (27)

as well as an additional three-body interaction,

WCS(3)​(𝐫,𝐫′,𝐫′′)=G​𝐫′′−𝐫|𝐫′′−𝐫|2⋅𝐫′′−𝐫′|𝐫′′−𝐫′|2,W^{(3)}_{\rm CS}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime\prime})=G\frac{{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime\prime}-{\mathbf{r}}}{|{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime\prime}-{\mathbf{r}}|^{2}}\cdot\frac{{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime\prime}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}}{|{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime\prime}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|^{2}}, (28)

where ω\omega denotes the frequency of the harmonic trap, while gg and GG represent the coupling strengths of the two-body inverse-square and three-body interaction terms, respectively. The exact expression for the wave function density simplifies considerably for the specific choice of coupling constants, g=G=2g=G=2 (see Appendix H). Therefore, we focus on the model with this parameter setting, considering a system of size L×LL\times L with L=10L=10 and an angular frequency of ω=1\omega=1. The resulting ground-state energies and particle numbers obtained from the converged TF ansatz, together with the corresponding exact values, are presented in Table 3. The ground state particle number density profile n⁡(r≡|𝐫|)n(r\equiv|{\mathbf{r}}|), obtained by averaging over the angular degrees of freedom, is shown in Fig. 5, further confirming that the proposed TF architecture accurately captures the ground state of two-dimensional systems, even in the presence of three-body interactions.

III.3 Harmonically Confined Bosons with Gaussian Interactions

We next consider a system of identical bosons confined in the two-dimensional isotropic harmonic trap defined in Eq. (27) and interacting via a Gaussian-shaped potential:

WGS​(𝐫,𝐫′)=gπ​s2​e−|𝐫−𝐫′|2s2,W_{\rm GS}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\frac{g}{\pi s^{2}}\,\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|^{2}}{s^{2}}}, (29)

where gg denotes the interaction strength, and ss characterizes the range of the interaction.

Small systems with a fixed particle number, N=2N=2 to N=4N=4, can be exactly diagonalized as shown in Ref. [45]. By setting the probabilities p±p_{\pm} for changing the particle number in the MCMC sampling algorithm (see Sec. II.4) to zero, the TF ansatz can be used to determine the ground state of the system within the canonical ensemble. As shown in Fig. 6, the TF ansatz accurately reproduces the ground-state energies obtained from ED calculations.

The ground-state condensate fraction of the confined bosons can also be extracted as the largest eigenvalue of the OBDM [47]. However, in the absence of translational invariance, the OBDM no longer depends solely on the relative displacement, making its estimation considerably more complex and computationally challenging (see Appendix F). One possible approach to avoid its direct evaluation is to employ the so-called natural orbitals, which play a role similar to marginal distributions for probability densities [50]. The idea is to project the OBDM onto an orthogonal basis set of single-particle orbitals {ϕ1​(𝐫),…,ϕM​(𝐫)}\{\phi_{1}({\mathbf{r}}),\ldots,\phi_{M}({\mathbf{r}})\}, such that the elements of the projected OBDM, ρi​j\rho_{ij}, are given by

ρi​j=∫d𝐫​d𝐫′​ϕi​(𝐫)​ϕj​(𝐫′)​ρ​(𝐫,𝐫′).\rho_{ij}=\int\differential{\mathbf{r}}\,\differential{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}\,\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\,\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\,\rho({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}). (30)

A Monte Carlo estimator for ρi​j\rho_{ij} can then be written as [50]:

ρi​j=𝔼𝐫n∼|φ¯n|2𝔼𝐫′∼ρ​[ϕi​(𝐫)​ϕj​(𝐫′)​φn​(𝐫′,𝐫2,…,𝐫n)ρ⁡(𝐫′)​φn​(𝐫,𝐫2,…,𝐫n)],\rho_{ij}=\EX_{{\mathbf{r}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\EX_{{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}\sim\rho}\biggl[\frac{\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\,\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\,\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{r}}_{n})}{\rho({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\,\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{r}}_{n})}\biggr], (31)

where ρ\rho is an arbitrary probability distribution over single-particle states. In practice, we take ρ\rho to be the ground-state density of a single harmonically trapped boson, while the natural orbitals |nx,ny⟩\ket{n_x,n_y} are chosen as the eigenstates of the two-dimensional harmonic oscillator.

The resulting condensate fraction obtained from this estimator is shown in Fig. 6. The excellent agreement with the ED results demonstrates the accuracy and effectiveness of the OBDM projection approach. Crucially, the ansatz enables us to extend the analysis beyond ED limits, yielding results for systems of up to N=10N=10 bosons.

We next analyze the same system within the grand-canonical ensemble. By varying the chemical potential μ\mu and the interaction strength gg, while keeping the interaction range fixed at s=0.5s=0.5, we obtain the phase diagram shown in Fig. 7. As might be expected, the ground-state particle number increases with the chemical potential, and this growth is suppressed as the interaction strength is increased. In contrast, the condensate fraction remains relatively large over the entire range of μ\mu for weak interactions but decreases significantly as gg and μ\mu become large together. The ground state particle number density, displayed in the insets of Fig. 7, confirms that our ansatz accurately captures the ground state while preserving the required radial symmetry.

IV Conclusion

We have introduced a symmetric variational state for bosonic theories. The state makes use of the transformer architecture and its masking mechanism to parameterize the amplitudes of configurations with varying boson numbers using a universal set of variational parameters. Our trial wavefunction handles particle interactions using the attention mechanism in each block, offering a controllable and systematically improvable architecture. Because the state is particle-number agnostic, it can naturally be used for grand canonical open systems, where equilibrium is maintained as particles are exchanged with a bath under a fixed chemical potential μ\mu. Focusing on many-boson systems in two dimensions, we demonstrate a computationally efficient VMC solver.

First-principles estimation of grand canonical states is a key ingredient in the study of systems where the phase diagram is probed by tuning the chemical potential, while the total number of particles may be difficult to control. Away from the thermodynamic limit, statistical ensembles are not equivalent, creating the need for an extension of the VMC toolbox to the grand canonical ensemble. The NQS pipeline is well-placed to address these ab-initio computational challenges. Having become the default choice in most classical AI applications, variational states based on the transformer architecture offer a universal and rapidly scalable computational framework to reach accurate descriptions of these systems.

Equilibrium properties of such bosonic systems can be precisely evaluated Path Integral Monte Carlo and worm algorithms [52, 5, 6]. However, these traditional methods face severe limitations when computing real-time dynamics due to the dynamical sign problem [18]. Explicit analytical trial states such as our transformer-based architecture can be extended using the Time-Dependent Variational Principle (TDVP). This clears the way to the study of real-time dynamics directly in continuous space.

Our variational approach is well suited to investigate cosmological phenomena simulated in ultracold atomic condensates, such as analog false vacuum decay [9]. Standard theoretical approaches to these setups rely on the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, which is limited by mean field truncation. Describing quantum tunneling and non-Gaussian fluctuations is difficult in the mean field language. On-demand access to accurate estimates of density profiles and the one-body density matrix can also be used for direct comparison with modern experiments [9, 7, 16, 17], helping to reveal new physics through parameter estimation and system control. Taking advantage of expressive modern trial states in VMC opens the door to the next generation of precision modeling of grand-canonical systems.

Software and simulations

All simulations were performed on Nvidia L40 graphical processing units using the JAX [8] library for array manipulation and automatic differentiation. Neural network design was conducted using Flax [26]. Optax [20] was used for optimization. NumPy [25] and SciPy [60] were utilized for data processing, and plots were produced using Matplotlib [30]. The codes used to run the simulations and reproduce the examples presented in this paper are available on GitHub in Ref. [29].

Appendix A Architecture

In this work, we propose an alternative neural network ansatz, based on the well-known Transformer (TF) architecture, originally introduced as a deep learning model in 2017 [59]. The core mechanism that learns correlations by assigning weights to each pair of inputs is the so-called self-attention mechanism. This mechanism plays a particularly crucial role in our case, as it ensures the permutation invariance of the architecture with respect to its input – a fundamental requirement for representing bosonic wavefunctions. A single layer of the TF model, as illustrated in Fig. 2, contains a masked multi-head self-attention component composed of HH independent self-attention heads. Each head is parameterized independently and operates on the input in parallel, allowing the model to learn correlations across multiple scales, while a mask is used to exclude inputs corresponding to non-existent particles. The output of the multi-head self-attention component is obtained by concatenating the outputs of all individual attention heads, resulting in a tensor of the same shape (nmax,k)(n_{\rm max},k) as the input. To enhance the representational power of the model, the multi-head self-attention block is followed by linear layers, which act independently on each input position. Additionally, to ensure the stability of the model, skip connections and layer normalization are employed in each layer.

The final TF architecture is illustrated in Fig. 2. Initially, the input is transformed using an embedding function and is then processed by a stack of LL identical TF layers. Each layer consists of a MHA sub-layer with HH heads. The weights of the MHA matrices and the linear layers are shared between all particle positions but are independently learned for each layer ll. The exact specification of trainable parameters, including the number of attention heads, transformer layers, and the typical embedding dimension, is summarized in Table 4. In practice, we typically choose L=2L=2 and H=4H=4.

After passing through all TF layers, the output tensor retains the same shape as the input to the first TF layer, that is, (n,k)(n,k). To obtain the nn-particle wavefunction φn​(𝐑n)\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}), this tensor must be projected into a single scalar value. We begin by reducing along the first dimension, which corresponds to the number of particles, using the LogSumExp function. The resulting vector of shape (k,)(k,) is then mapped to a scalar through a feed-forward neural network.

LogSumExp​(x)=log⁡(∑i=1kai​exi)\text{LogSumExp}(x)=\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}e^{x_{i}}\right) (32)

It is worth noting that throughout the entire TF architecture, we employ the LogCosh activation function, in contrast to the Tanh activation function used in the DS architecture. The network weights are initialized using the Xavier uniform initialization method, which is designed to maintain the variance of activations across layers. Bias terms are initialized to zero throughout the network.

Appendix B Additional factors

The additional factors must be incorporated into the ansatz to facilitate its optimization. In the following section, we analyze three categories of such factors, originally introduced in Ref. [41]. Some of these enable the incorporation of physical constraints of the system under study, while others are intended to enhance convergence during the optimization.

B.1 Cutoff Factor

The cutoff factor is used to enforce closed boundary conditions within the system. These conditions require that the nn-particle wave function vanishes as any particle approaches the boundary of the system. To satisfy this constraint, the ansatz is multiplied by a factor that ensures the wave function tends to zero at the boundaries.

In the one-dimensional case, where the system is defined on the interval (0,L)(0,L), the cutoff factor takes the following form:

(L30)−n/2∏i=1nxiL(1−xiL).\left(\frac{L}{30}\right)^{-n/2}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{x_{i}}{L}\left(1-\frac{x_{i}}{L}\right). (33)

In the two-dimensional case, the system is defined on the square domain (0,L)×(0,L)(0,L)\times(0,L), and the cutoff factor is accordingly adapted to vanish at all boundaries:

(L100)−n​∏i=1nxiL​(1−xiL)​∏i=1nyiL​(1−yiL),\left(\frac{L}{100}\right)^{-n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{x_{i}}{L}\left(1-\frac{x_{i}}{L}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{y_{i}}{L}\left(1-\frac{y_{i}}{L}\right), (34)

where single particle position 𝐫i=(xi,yi){\mathbf{r}}_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i}) and the normalization in front is included for stable optimization across different particle number sectors [41]. In the case of periodic boundary conditions, the periodicity of the system is already incorporated into the embedding function (see Sec. II.2). Therefore, no additional cutoff factor is required.

B.2 Particle number distribution factor

We additionally incorporate a parameterizable regularization factor qnq_{n} into the nn-particle wave function to ensure a well-behaved particle-number distribution. This factor is defined as a smoothed rectangular pulse that decays exponentially outside a central window:

qn=11+e−s⁡(n−c1)⋅11+es⁡(n−c2),0≤c1≤c2,s>0.q_{n}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-s(n-c_{1})}}\cdot\frac{1}{1+e^{s(n-c_{2})}},\quad 0\leq c_{1}\leq c_{2},\quad s>0. (35)

The purpose of this factor is to confine the most probable values of the particle number nn to the finite interval [c1,c2][c_{1},c_{2}]. In practice, the parameters c1c_{1}, c2c_{2}, and ss are optimized together with the rest of the ansatz parameters using a gradient-based optimization algorithm, typically with a higher learning rate.

B.3 Jastrow Factor

In some of the models considered in this work, the two-body interaction potential W⁡(𝐫i,𝐫j)W({\mathbf{r}}_{i},{\mathbf{r}}_{j}) diverges for a configuration 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} in which two particles approach one another, 𝐫i→𝐫j{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\rightarrow{\mathbf{r}}_{j}. For the exact ground-state wave function, this divergence is typically canceled by a corresponding divergence in the kinetic energy. However, since the ansatz is only an approximation to the true ground state, the local energy Enloc​(𝐑n)E^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) for such configurations may still exhibit divergences. These divergences can lead to large oscillations in the estimated energy during MCMC sampling, thereby complicating convergence to the true ground state.

To address this issue, we incorporate the correct short-range cusp behavior into the variational ansatz, thereby enforcing Kato’s cusp condition [23], which ensures that the local energy remains finite as 𝐫i→𝐫j{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\rightarrow{\mathbf{r}}_{j}. This can be achieved without explicit knowledge of the exact many-body ground state by analyzing the corresponding two-body problem and imposing the requirement:

lim𝐫i→𝐫jEnloc​(𝐑n)=lim𝐫i→𝐫jH​φn​(𝐑n)φn​(𝐑n)<∞.\lim_{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\rightarrow{\mathbf{r}}_{j}}E^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\lim_{{\mathbf{r}}_{i}\rightarrow{\mathbf{r}}_{j}}\frac{H\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}{\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}<\infty. (36)

The Jastrow factors for the Lieb–Liniger model and the one-dimensional Calogero–Sutherland model were derived in Ref. [41]. For the reader’s convenience, we present only the final expressions here:

JnLL​(Xn)=∏i<jn(1L​|xi−xj|+1m​g​L),J^{\text{LL}}_{n}(X_{n})=\prod_{i<j}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{L}|x_{i}-x_{j}|+\frac{1}{mgL}\right), (37)
JnCS​(Xn)=∏i<jn(1L​|xi−xj|)λ⋅(1−1L​|xi−xj|)λ,J^{\text{CS}}_{n}(X_{n})=\prod_{i<j}^{n}\left(\frac{1}{L}|x_{i}-x_{j}|\right)^{\lambda}\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{L}|x_{i}-x_{j}|\right)^{\lambda}, (38)

where λ=12(1+1+4​m​g)\lambda=\frac{1}{2}\biggr(1+\sqrt{1+4mg}\biggr).

The Jastrow factor for the inverse-square two-body potential W⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=g/|𝐫−𝐫′|2W({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=g/|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|^{2} in the two-dimensional Calogero–Sutherland model can be derived in an analogous manner. We begin by considering only the radial part of the Laplacian expressed in polar coordinates:

∇2f=∂2f∂r2+1r​∂f∂r.\nabla^{2}f=\frac{\partial^{2}f}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}. (39)

The corresponding cusp condition for the inverse-square interaction then takes the form

−(∂2∂r2+1r​∂∂r)​u​(|𝐫|)+g​u⁡(|𝐫|)r2=0.-\left(\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\right)u(|{\mathbf{r}}|)+g\frac{u(|{\mathbf{r}}|)}{r^{2}}=0. (40)

This condition is satisfied by the trial function u⁡(|𝐫|)=|𝐫|λu(|{\mathbf{r}}|)=|{\mathbf{r}}|^{\lambda} with the choice λ=m​g=g/2\lambda=\sqrt{mg}=\sqrt{g/2}. Consequently, the Jastrow factor for the two-dimensional Calogero–Sutherland model is given by

JnCS​(𝐑n)=∏i<jn|𝐫i−𝐫j|λ.J^{\text{CS}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\prod_{i<j}^{n}|{\mathbf{r}}_{i}-{\mathbf{r}}_{j}|^{\lambda}. (41)

Although our derivation of the Jastrow factor accounts only for two-body inverse-square interactions and neglects the stronger three-body divergence that arises when three particles simultaneously approach one another, the resulting factor is nevertheless sufficient in practice to suppress large oscillations in the local energy.

Appendix C VMC in Fock space

In a standard Variational Monte Carlo (VMC), the characterization of the physical properties of many-body system requires the efficient computation of expectation values of the form:

⟨Q⟩=⟨ψθ|Q|ψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩\langle Q\rangle=\frac{\langle\psi_{\theta}|Q|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle} (42)

where |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle is a variational many-body state defined by amplitudes ψθ​(𝐱)\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) in a basis 𝐱\mathbf{x}, while QQ is a generic operator like Hamiltonian or one-body density operator. The direct calculation of the expectation value in numerator and denominator cannot be performed exactly, however, estimates can be made through Monte Carlo integration. In general, we can rewrite the expectation in Eq. (42) as

⟨Q⟩=∫d​𝐱​⟨ψθ|𝐱⟩​⟨𝐱|Q|ψθ⟩∫d​𝐱′​|ψθ​(𝐱)|2=∫d​𝐱​pθ​(𝐱)​QL​(𝐱)\langle Q\rangle=\frac{\int d\mathbf{x}\langle\psi_{\theta}|\mathbf{x}\rangle\langle\mathbf{x}|Q|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\int d\mathbf{x^{\prime}}|\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}}=\int d\mathbf{x}p_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})Q_{L}(\mathbf{x}) (43)

where

|φ¯​(𝐱)|2=|ψθ​(𝐱)|2∫d​𝐱′​|ψθ​(𝐱′)|2|\bar{\varphi}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}=\frac{|\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})|^{2}}{\int d\mathbf{x^{\prime}}|\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x^{\prime}})|^{2}} (44)

and the local observable function QL​(𝐱)Q_{L}(\mathbf{x}) is defined as:

QL​(𝐱)=⟨𝐱|Q|ψθ⟩⟨𝐱|ψθ⟩Q_{L}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\langle\mathbf{x}|Q|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\mathbf{x}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle} (45)

The unbiased estimator to the expectation value of QLQ_{L} can then obtained as the empirical average of the associated local observable QLQ_{L} evaluated at configurations 𝐱𝐢\mathbf{x_{i}}:

⟨Q⟩=𝔼𝐱∼|φ¯​(x)|2[QL(𝐱)]≈1Ns∑i=1NsQL(𝐱𝐢)\langle Q\rangle=\EX_{\mathbf{x}\sim|\bar{\varphi}(x)|^{2}}\biggr[Q_{L}(\mathbf{x})\biggr]\approx\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}Q_{L}(\mathbf{x_{i}}) (46)

An analogous method for estimating observables in the context of QFTs was developed in Ref. [41]. The approach, referred to as VMC in Fock space, expresses the expectation value of an nn-particle local observable function Qnloc​(𝐑n)Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) for a quantum field state |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle, as

⟨Q⟩=⟨Ψ|Q|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=𝔼n∼Pn𝔼𝐑n∼|φ¯n|2[Qnloc(𝐑n)],\langle Q\rangle=\frac{\langle\Psi|Q|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}=\EX_{n\sim P_{n}}\EX_{{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\biggr[Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})\biggr]\,, (47)

where the n-particle local observable of the configuration 𝐑n={𝐫1,𝐫2,…,𝐫n}{\mathbf{R}}_{n}=\{{\mathbf{r}}_{1},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},\dots,{\mathbf{r}}_{n}\} is

Qnloc​(𝐑n)=⟨𝐑n|Q|Ψ⟩⟨𝐑n|Ψ⟩Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\frac{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|Q|\Psi\rangle}{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|\Psi\rangle} (48)

with the probability distribution of the particle number

Pn=⟨φn|φn⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩=∫dn𝐫​|φn​(𝐑n)|2∑m=0∞∫dn𝐫′​|φm​(𝐑m′)|2P_{n}=\frac{\langle\varphi_{n}|\varphi_{n}\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}=\frac{\int\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}{\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\int\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{m}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{m})|^{2}} (49)

and the probability distribution of the n-particle wave function

|φ¯n​(𝐑n)|2=|φn​(𝐑n)|2∫dn𝐫′​|φn​(𝐑n′)|2.|\bar{\varphi}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}=\frac{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}{\int\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{n})|^{2}}\,. (50)

The above approach can be seen as a natural generalization of the traditional VMC, where the expectation value is extended to include both the distribution of the nn-particle wave function and the particle number distribution. The unbiased estimator to the expectation value of Qnloc​(𝐑n)Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) can then obtained as the empirical average of Qnloc​(𝐑n)Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) evaluated at configurations 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} drawn jointly from PnP_{n} and |φ¯n​(𝐑n)|2|\bar{\varphi}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}:

⟨Q⟩=𝔼n∼Pn𝔼𝐑n∼|φ¯n|2[Qnloc(𝐑n)]≈1∑nNn∑n∑in=1NnQnloc(𝐑n(in))\langle Q\rangle=\EX_{n\sim P_{n}}\EX_{{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\biggr[Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})\biggr]\approx\frac{1}{\sum_{n}N_{n}}\sum_{n}\sum_{i_{n}=1}^{N_{n}}Q^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{(i_{n})}) (51)

We next demonstrate that the developed VMC formalism in Fock space can be effectively applied to estimate key physical observables required for the optimization. Furthermore, in Appendix F, we show that it is capable of estimating practically useful quantities, such as the one-body density matrix and the condensate fraction.

Appendix D Stochastic optimization

The goal of VMC is to minimize the energy expectation value with respect to the trial state |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle by finding the optimal variational parameters

θopt=argminθE​(θ)=argminθ⟨ψθ|H|ψθ⟩⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩≥E0,\theta_{\text{opt}}=\argmin_{\theta}E(\theta)=\argmin_{\theta}\frac{\langle\psi_{\theta}|H|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}{\langle\psi_{\theta}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle}\geq E_{0}\,, (52)

where E0E_{0} is the true ground state energy. Standard gradient-based optimization methods can be employed to determine the optimal parameters θopt\theta_{\text{opt}} by iteratively updating the parameters using the gradient g=∇θE​(θ)g=\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta), starting from an initial guess. However, a more general optimization approach, motivated by physical principles, is based on imaginary-time evolution. We next present an overview of this approach, which closely follows Ref. [42], where the topic is discussed in greater detail.

Imaginary-time evolution is a well-known technique that exponentially suppresses the higher-energy components of an arbitrary trial state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle, such that the ground-state component |0⟩|0\rangle dominates in the long-time limit:

|ψ⁡(τ)⟩=e−τ​H​|ψ⟩\displaystyle|\psi(\tau)\rangle=e^{-\tau H}|\psi\rangle =∑ncn​e−τ​En​|n⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{n}c_{n}e^{-\tau E_{n}}|n\rangle
∝|0⟩+∑n>0cnc0​e−τ⁡(En−E0)​|n⟩→τ→∞|0⟩\displaystyle\propto|0\rangle+\sum_{n>0}\frac{c_{n}}{c_{0}}e^{-\tau(E_{n}-E_{0})}|n\rangle\xrightarrow{\tau\to\infty}|0\rangle (53)

assuming that the trial state is not orthogonal to the ground state, such that c0=⟨0|ψ⟩≠0c_{0}=\langle 0|\psi\rangle\neq 0.

We then consider the imaginary-time evolution of the trial state |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle over a small time interval δ​τ\delta\tau, governed by the operator e−δ​τ​H^e^{-\delta\tau\hat{H}}. This evolution is equivalent to an update of the variational parameters θ→θ′=θ+δ​θ\theta\to\theta^{\prime}=\theta+\delta\theta, such that:

|ψθ+δ​θ⟩≈e−δ​τ​H​|ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta+\delta\theta}\rangle\approx e^{-\delta\tau H}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle (54)

Expanding both sides of Eq. (54) to first order in the small parameter increments and taking the limit δ​τ→0\delta\tau\to 0, we obtain:

S​θ˙=−gS\dot{\theta}=-g (55)

where θ˙=d​θ/d​τ\dot{\theta}=d\theta/d\tau and

Sμ​ν=2​Re⁡{⟨Oμ†​Oν⟩−⟨Oμ†⟩​⟨Oν⟩}=2​Re⁡{⟨Oμ†​(Oν−⟨Oν⟩)⟩}S_{\mu\nu}=2\operatorname{Re}\big\{\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}O_{\nu}\rangle-\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}\rangle\langle O_{\nu}\rangle\big\}=2\operatorname{Re}\big\{\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}(O_{\nu}-\langle O_{\nu}\rangle)\rangle\big\} (56)
gμ=2​Re⁡{⟨Oμ†​H⟩−⟨Oμ†⟩​⟨H⟩}=2​Re⁡{⟨Oμ†​(E−⟨E⟩)⟩}g_{\mu}=2\operatorname{Re}\big\{\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}H\rangle-\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}\rangle\langle H\rangle\big\}=2\operatorname{Re}\big\{\langle O_{\mu}^{\dagger}(E-\langle E\rangle)\rangle\big\} (57)

Here, g=∇θE​(θ)g=\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta) denotes the energy gradient with respect to the variational parameters, while the matrix SS is commonly referred to as the quantum geometric tensor (QGT) or the quantum Fisher information matrix [3]. The indices μ\mu and ν\nu label the variational parameters and the expectation values ⟨⋅⟩≡⟨ψθ|⋅|ψθ⟩/⟨ψθ|ψθ⟩\langle\cdot\rangle\equiv\langle\psi_{\theta}|\cdot|\psi_{\theta}\rangle/\langle\psi_{\theta}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle are evaluated with respect to the normalized trial state |ψθ⟩|\psi_{\theta}\rangle at imaginary time τ\tau. Diagonal operators OμO_{\mu} are defined as

Oμ​|ψθ⟩=∂θμ|ψθ⟩.O_{\mu}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle=\partial_{\theta^{\mu}}|\psi_{\theta}\rangle\,. (58)

The gradient and the S-matrix defined in Eqs. 56 and 57 depend only on the local energy Eloc​(𝐑n)E^{\text{loc}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) and the local operator Oνloc​(𝐑n)O^{\text{loc}}_{\nu}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}), which are sampled using the MCMC technique described in the previous section. The corresponding expectation values ⟨E⟩\langle E\rangle and ⟨Oν⟩\langle O_{\nu}\rangle can be further evaluated as empirical means over all sampled configurations 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n}. This enables the estimation of the gradient gg and the S-matrix required for optimizing the model parameters, without the need for direct evaluation of ∇θE​(θ)\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta).

Since the Eq. (55) reduces to the explicit inversion of the S-matrix (known as stochastic reconfiguration (SR) update rule), the approach is computationally expensive for large models, as it requires solving an Np×NpN_{p}\times N_{p} linear system at each iteration, where NpN_{p} denotes the number of model parameters. To mitigate this cost, one can employ a computational trick introduced in Ref. [15]. Specifically, by utilizing the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, Eq. (55) can be reformulated as

θ˙=S−1​g=(O¯†​O¯)−1​O¯†​ϵ¯=O¯†​(O¯​O¯†)−1​ϵ¯.\dot{\theta}=S^{-1}g=(\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{O})^{-1}\bar{O}^{\dagger}\bar{\epsilon}=\bar{O}^{\dagger}(\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger})^{-1}\bar{\epsilon}\;. (59)

In the final expression, the rank of the S-matrix is at most NsN_{s} and, consequently, the matrix size reduces from Np×NpN_{p}\times N_{p} to Ns×NsN_{s}\times N_{s}. This method is therefore particularly useful for large models where the number of parameters NpN_{p} significantly exceeds the total number of samples per iteration NsN_{s}. Following the Ref. [41], we introduce the neural tangent kernel, defined as:

T=O¯​O¯†T=\bar{O}\bar{O}^{\dagger} (60)

where we defined centered and normalized variables:

ϵ¯=(Eloc​(𝐑n)−⟨E⟩)/Ns\bar{\epsilon}=(E^{\text{loc}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})-\langle E\rangle)/\sqrt{N_{s}} (61)
O¯ν=(Oνloc​(𝐑n)−⟨Oν⟩)/Ns\bar{O}_{\nu}=(O^{\text{loc}}_{\nu}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})-\langle O_{\nu}\rangle)/\sqrt{N_{s}} (62)

while the term Oνloc​(𝐑n)O^{\text{loc}}_{\nu}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) can be directly evaluated as

Oνloc​(𝐑n)\displaystyle O^{\text{loc}}_{\nu}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) =1⟨𝐑n|Ψ⟩⟨𝐑n|∫d𝐫ψ^†(𝐫)∂νψ^(𝐫)|Ψ⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|\Psi\rangle}\biggr\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\biggr|\int\differential{\mathbf{r}}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\partial_{\nu}\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}})\biggr|\Psi\biggr\rangle
=1ϕn​(𝐑n)​∂νϕn​(𝐑n)=∂νln⁡ϕn​(𝐑n).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\partial_{\nu}\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\partial_{\nu}\ln\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}). (63)

For the Hamiltonian under consideration, the local energy Eloc​(𝐑n)E^{\text{loc}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) can be decomposed into distinct contributions, including the kinetic energy, potential energy, and interaction energy terms:

Eloc​(𝐑n)=⟨𝐑n|H|Ψ⟩⟨𝐑n|Ψ⟩=Ekinloc​(𝐑n)+Vextloc​(𝐑n)+W2-bodyloc​(𝐑n)E^{\text{loc}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\frac{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|H|\Psi\rangle}{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|\Psi\rangle}=E^{\text{loc}}_{\text{kin}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})+V^{\text{loc}}_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})+W^{\text{loc}}_{\text{2-body}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) (64)

=(−12​m)​1ϕn​(𝐑n)​∇2ϕn​(𝐑n)\displaystyle=\left(-\frac{1}{2m}\right)\frac{1}{\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\nabla^{2}\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})
=−12​m(∇2lnϕn(𝐑n)+(∇lnϕn(𝐑n))2)\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2m}\left(\nabla^{2}\ln\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})+\left(\nabla\ln\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})\right)^{2}\right) (65)

The expectation value of the local external and chemical potential terms may be expressed as

Vextloc​(𝐑n)\displaystyle V^{\text{loc}}_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) =1⟨𝐑n|Ψ⟩⟨𝐑n|∫d𝐫ψ^†(𝐫)(V(𝐫)−μ)ψ^(𝐫)|Ψ⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|\Psi\rangle}\biggr\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\biggr|\int d{\mathbf{r}}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\biggr(V({\mathbf{r}})-\mu\biggr)\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}})\biggr|\Psi\biggr\rangle
=1ϕn​(𝐑n)∑i=1n(V(𝐫i)−μ)ϕn(𝐑n)=∑i=1n(V(𝐫i)−μ),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\biggr(V({\mathbf{r}}_{i})-\mu\biggr)\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\biggr(V({\mathbf{r}}_{i})-\mu\biggr)\,, (66)

while the expectation value of the local two-body interaction potential term is

W2-bodyloc​(𝐑n)\displaystyle W^{\text{loc}}_{\text{2-body}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) =1⟨𝐑n|Ψ⟩⟨𝐑n|∫d𝐫d𝐫′ψ^†(𝐫)ψ^†(𝐫′)W(𝐫−𝐫′)ψ^(𝐫′)ψ^(𝐫)|Ψ⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}|\Psi\rangle}\biggr\langle{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\biggr|\int\differential{\mathbf{r}}\differential{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})W({\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}})\biggr|\Psi\biggr\rangle
=1ϕn​(𝐑n)​∑i<jnW⁡(𝐫i−𝐫j)​ϕn​(𝐑n)=∑i<jnW⁡(𝐫i−𝐫j)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\sum_{i<j}^{n}W({\mathbf{r}}_{i}-{\mathbf{r}}_{j})\phi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\sum_{i<j}^{n}W({\mathbf{r}}_{i}-{\mathbf{r}}_{j}) (67)

The derived expression requires computing the gradient and Laplacian of the logarithm of the n-particle wave function amplitude, which is provided as output of our ansatz.

If we approximate S≈𝕀S\approx\mathbb{I} in Eq. (55), we obtain the standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimization rule:

θ′=θ−δ​τ​∇θE​(θ)\theta^{\prime}=\theta-\delta\tau\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta) (68)

Now, we can use any of the popular optimizers from deep learning, such as Adam [33]. This method is the least computationally demanding and was employed in Ref. [41]. However, it often converges to higher ground state energies compared to the SR (minSR) methods, or may even fail to converge for large systems.

Appendix E MCMC in Fock space

To generate the samples {𝐑i:i=1,…,Ns}\{{\mathbf{R}}_{i}:i=1,\dots,N_{s}\} required for evaluating the observables in Eq. (51), it is standard practice to employ established Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. In the case of Fock-space VMC, the algorithm must be generalized to sample jointly from PnP_{n} and |φ¯n|2|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}. This extension can be regarded as a generalization of standard MCMC sampling in the classical grand-canonical ensemble to the quantum grand-canonical ensemble. In this work, we largely follow the sampling strategy introduced in Ref. [41], extending it to the case of d≥1d\geq 1.

As in conventional MCMC algorithms, the procedure in Fock space begins by proposing a new configuration 𝐑n′{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime} from the current configuration 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n}. The proposed configuration is then accepted or rejected according to the Metropolis–Hastings probability:

paccept=min⁡(1,Pbos​(𝐑n′)Pbos​(𝐑n)​g⁡(𝐑n|𝐑n′)g⁡(𝐑n′|𝐑n)),p_{\text{accept}}=\min\Biggl(1,\frac{P_{\text{bos}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime})}{P_{\text{bos}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\frac{g({\mathbf{R}}_{n}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime})}{g({\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\Biggr), (69)

where g⁡(𝐑n′|𝐑n)g({\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n}) denotes the transition probability from 𝐑n→𝐑n′{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime} under the chosen proposal scheme, and the probability of a configuration 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} is given by

P⁡(𝐑n)\displaystyle P({\mathbf{R}}_{n}) =Pn⋅|φ¯n|2dn𝐑\displaystyle=P_{n}\cdot|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}\differential^{n}{\mathbf{R}}
=∫dn𝐫′​|φn​(𝐑n′)|2∑m∫dm𝐫′​|φm​(𝐑m′)|2⋅|φn​(𝐑n)|2∫dn𝐫′​|φn​(𝐑n′)|2dn𝐑\displaystyle=\frac{\int\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{n})|^{2}}{\sum_{m}\int\differential^{m}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{m}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{m})|^{2}}\cdot\frac{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}{\int\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{n})|^{2}}\differential^{n}{\mathbf{R}}
=|φn​(𝐑n)|2​dn𝐑∑m∫dm𝐫′​|φm​(𝐑m′)|2,\displaystyle=\frac{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}\differential^{n}{\mathbf{R}}}{\sum_{m}\int\differential^{m}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{m}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{m})|^{2}}, (70)

where the definitions of PnP_{n} from Eq. (49) and φ¯n\bar{\varphi}_{n} from Eq. (50) have been used.

Because we focus on bosonic states, each configuration 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} is physically indistinguishable from any of its permutations 𝐑n′′∈Sym​(𝐑n){\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime\prime}\in\text{Sym}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}). Accordingly, the probability associated with a bosonic configuration 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} is

Pbos​(𝐑n)=∑𝐑n′′∈Sym​(𝐑n)P⁡(𝐑n′′)=n!​|φn​(𝐑n)|2​dn𝐫∑m∫dm𝐫′​|φm​(𝐑m′)|2.P_{\text{bos}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})=\sum_{{\mathbf{R}}^{\prime\prime}_{n}\in\text{Sym}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}P({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime\prime}_{n})=\frac{n!|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}}{\sum_{m}\int\differential^{m}{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\varphi_{m}({\mathbf{R}}^{\prime}_{m})|^{2}}. (71)

We next specify the proposal scheme, which enables us to generate new bosonic configurations 𝐑n′{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime} and also allows for changes in particle number. With probability 2​p±2p_{\pm}, the scheme proposes configurations with particle number increased or decreased, each with equal probability p±p_{\pm}. With the remaining probability p0=1−2​p±p_{0}=1-2p_{\pm}, the particle number is preserved, and a uniform random displacement is applied to all particle positions:

𝐑n→𝐑n′=𝐑n+𝜻,{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime}={\mathbf{R}}_{n}+\bm{\zeta}, (72)

where 𝜻∼U⁡([−w2,w2]d)\bm{\zeta}\sim U\left([-\tfrac{w}{2},\tfrac{w}{2}]^{d}\right) is a dd-dimensional uniform random vector of width ww. In this case only, the transition rule is symmetric, i.e., g⁡(𝐑n|𝐑n′)=g⁡(𝐑n′|𝐑n)g({\mathbf{R}}_{n}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime})=g({\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n}), so the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability for the transition 𝐑n→𝐑n′{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime} reduces to

paccept=min⁡(1,|φn​(𝐑n′)|2|φn​(𝐑n)|2).p_{\text{accept}}=\min\Biggl(1,\frac{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{\prime})|^{2}}{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}\Biggr). (73)

On the other hand, with probability p±p_{\pm}, the proposal function either adds or removes a particle. In the case of particle addition, a new particle is introduced at a position 𝐫n+1{\mathbf{r}}_{n+1}, which is sampled uniformly at random from the domain [0,L]d[0,L]^{d}. With the same probability p±p_{\pm}, a particle is removed by selecting an index i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\} uniformly at random. These proposals are not symmetric: for particle addition, the proposal probability is

g⁡(𝐑n+1|𝐑n)=p±⋅d𝐫n+1Ld,g({\mathbf{R}}_{n+1}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n})=p_{\pm}\cdot\frac{\differential{\mathbf{r}}_{n+1}}{L^{d}}, (74)

while for particle removal it is

g⁡(𝐑n−1|𝐑n)=p±⋅1n.g({\mathbf{R}}_{n-1}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n})=p_{\pm}\cdot\frac{1}{n}. (75)

Hence, the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability for adding a particle, i.e., for the transition 𝐑n→𝐑n+1{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathbf{R}}_{n+1}, is

paccept\displaystyle p_{\text{accept}} =min⁡(1,Pbos​(𝐑n+1)Pbos​(𝐑n)⋅g⁡(𝐑n|𝐑n+1)g⁡(𝐑n+1|𝐑n))\displaystyle=\min\left(1,\frac{P_{\text{bos}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n+1})}{P_{\text{bos}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\cdot\frac{g({\mathbf{R}}_{n}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n+1})}{g({\mathbf{R}}_{n+1}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\right)
=min⁡(1,(n+1)!​|φn+1​(𝐑n+1)|2​dn+1𝐫n!​|φn​(𝐑n)|2​dn𝐫⋅p±n+1⋅Ldp±​d𝐫n+1)\displaystyle=\min\left(1,\frac{(n+1)!\,|\varphi_{n+1}({\mathbf{R}}_{n+1})|^{2}\,\differential^{n+1}{\mathbf{r}}}{n!\,|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}\,\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}}\cdot\frac{p_{\pm}}{n+1}\cdot\frac{L^{d}}{p_{\pm}\,\differential{\mathbf{r}}_{n+1}}\right)
=min⁡(1,Ld⋅|φn+1​(𝐑n+1)|2|φn​(𝐑n)|2),\displaystyle=\min\left(1,\frac{L^{d}\cdot|\varphi_{n+1}({\mathbf{R}}_{n+1})|^{2}}{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}\right)\,, (76)

while the acceptance probability for removing a particle, i.e., 𝐑n→𝐑n−1{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\rightarrow{\mathbf{R}}_{n-1}, is

paccept\displaystyle p_{\text{accept}} =min⁡(1,Pbos​(𝐑n−1)Pbos​(𝐑n)⋅g⁡(𝐑n|𝐑n−1)g⁡(𝐑n−1|𝐑n))\displaystyle=\min\left(1,\frac{P_{\text{bos}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n-1})}{P_{\text{bos}}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\cdot\frac{g({\mathbf{R}}_{n}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n-1})}{g({\mathbf{R}}_{n-1}|{\mathbf{R}}_{n})}\right)
=min⁡(1,(n−1)!​|φn−1​(𝐑n−1)|2​dn−1𝐫n!​|φn​(𝐑n)|2​dn𝐫⋅p±​d𝐫n−1Ld⋅np±)\displaystyle=\min\left(1,\frac{(n-1)!\,|\varphi_{n-1}({\mathbf{R}}_{n-1})|^{2}\,\differential^{n-1}{\mathbf{r}}}{n!\,|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}\,\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}}\cdot\frac{p_{\pm}\,\differential{\mathbf{r}}_{n-1}}{L^{d}}\cdot\frac{n}{p_{\pm}}\right)
=min⁡(1,1Ld⋅|φn−1​(𝐑n−1)|2|φn​(𝐑n)|2).\displaystyle=\min\left(1,\frac{1}{L^{d}}\cdot\frac{|\varphi_{n-1}({\mathbf{R}}_{n-1})|^{2}}{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})|^{2}}\right)\,. (77)

We typically set p±=0.25p_{\pm}=0.25, so that configurations with different particle numbers are proposed with probability 2​p±=50%2p_{\pm}=50\%. A larger value of p±p_{\pm} will force the algorithm to explore more particle-number sectors, which could significantly decrease the acceptance ratio. On the other hand, a smaller value of p±p_{\pm} enhances the algorithm’s ability to find optimal configurations within the same particle-number sector.

In practice, we run around 100 MCMC chains in parallel, using a sweep size (i.e., the number of Metropolis–Hastings steps performed before accepting a configuration as a valid sample) of 30 and collect 50 to 100 samples per chain. Expectation values are then estimated as empirical means over all collected samples.

Appendix F Estimation of observables

To verify that the ansatz correctly captures the ground state of the system, we compare not only the ground-state energy and particle number but also employ VMC to estimate additional observables, such as the ground-state particle-number density n⁡(𝐫)n({\mathbf{r}}) and the one-body density matrix ρ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)\rho({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}). In this section, we derive expressions for the observables analyzed in the main text.

F.1 Particle Number Density

The particle number density can be expressed as:

n⁡(𝐫)\displaystyle n({\mathbf{r}}) =1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|​ψ^†​(𝐫)​ψ^​(𝐫)​|Ψ⟩=1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ​|∫d⁡𝐫′​δ​(𝐫′−𝐫)​ψ^†​(𝐫′)​ψ^​(𝐫′)|​Ψ⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\langle\Psi|\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}})|\Psi\rangle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\langle\Psi|\int\differential{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}\;\delta({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}-{\mathbf{r}})\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})|\Psi\rangle
=1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩∑n=0∞∫dn𝐫|φn(𝐫n)|2(∑i=1nδ(𝐫−𝐫i))=1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩∑n=0∞∑i=1n∫dn\i𝐫|φn(𝐫n|𝐫i=𝐫)|2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\int\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}\;|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{n})|^{2}\biggr(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\delta({\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}_{i})\biggr)=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int\differential^{n\backslash i}{\mathbf{r}}\;|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{n}|{\mathbf{r}}_{i}={\mathbf{r}})|^{2}
=𝔼n∼Pn(∑i=1n𝔼𝐫n\i∼|φ¯n\i|2[|φn​(𝐫n|𝐫i=𝐫)|2∫d​𝐫i​|φn​(𝐫n)|2]),\displaystyle=\EX_{n\sim P_{n}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\EX_{{\mathbf{r}}_{n\backslash i}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n\backslash i}|^{2}}\left[\frac{|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{n}|{\mathbf{r}}_{i}={\mathbf{r}})|^{2}}{\int d{\mathbf{r}}_{i}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{n})|^{2}}\right]\right), (78)

where the second expectation value is taken over the marginal distribution |φ¯n\i|2=∫d⁡𝐫i​|φ¯n|2|\bar{\varphi}_{n\backslash i}|^{2}=\int\differential{\mathbf{r}}_{i}|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}, and the notation φn​(𝐑n|𝐫i=𝐫)\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}|{\mathbf{r}}_{i}={\mathbf{r}}) means that this function is evaluated at 𝐑n{\mathbf{R}}_{n} with the constraint that 𝐫i=𝐫{\mathbf{r}}_{i}={\mathbf{r}}. Samples from the marginal distribution may be obtained by sampling 𝐑n∼|φ¯n|2{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2} as usual, and ignoring 𝐫i{\mathbf{r}}_{i}.

F.2 One-body Density Matrix

In studying the ground state of a bosonic system, another very useful observable is the so-called one-body density matrix (OBDM), ρ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)\rho({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}), which can be expressed in terms of the particle creation and annihilation operators as

ρ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|​ψ^†​(𝐫′)​ψ^​(𝐫)​|Ψ⟩\rho({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\langle\Psi|\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}})|\Psi\rangle (79)

At zero-temperature, off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) is a key indicator of the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) phase. In the presence of ODLRO, the OBDM of the ground state |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle, approaches a nonzero plateau for large separations, that is, lim|𝐫−𝐫′|→∞ρ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=ρ0\lim_{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|\rightarrow\infty}\rho({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\rho_{0} where ρ0\rho_{0} is the condensate density [47].

F.2.1 Translation-invariant system

In a translationally invariant system, the OBDM depends only on the relative displacement vector 𝒔=|𝐫−𝐫′|\bm{s}=|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|:

ρ⁡(𝒔)\displaystyle\rho(\bm{s}) =1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​∑n=0∞n​∫dn−1𝐫​φn∗​(𝐫1+𝒔,𝐫2,…,𝐫N)​φn​(𝐫1,𝐫2,…,𝐫n)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\int\differential^{n-1}{\mathbf{r}}\varphi_{n}^{*}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}+\bm{s},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{N})\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{1},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{n})
=1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​∑n=0∞nLd​∫dn𝐫​φn∗​(𝐫1+𝒔,𝐫2,…,𝐫N)​φn​(𝐫1,𝐫2,…,𝐫n)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{n}{L^{d}}\int\differential^{n}{\mathbf{r}}\varphi_{n}^{*}({\mathbf{r}}_{1}+\bm{s},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{N})\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{1},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{n})
=𝔼n∼Pn𝔼𝐫n∼|φ¯n|2[nLdφn∗​(𝐫n|𝐫1=𝐫1+𝐬)φn​(𝐫n)].\displaystyle=\EX_{n\sim P_{n}}\EX_{{\mathbf{r}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\biggr[\frac{n}{L^{d}}\frac{\varphi_{n}^{*}({\mathbf{r}}_{n}|{\mathbf{r}}_{1}={\mathbf{r}}_{1}+\bm{s})}{\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{n})}\biggr]. (80)

This expression can now be straightforwardly evaluated as an empirical mean over configurations 𝐫n{\mathbf{r}}_{n} sampled jointly from PnP_{n} and |φ¯n|2|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}.

F.2.2 Inhomogeneous system

In the absence of translational invariance, the analysis becomes considerably more complex. The OBDM, expressed as an expectation value, is given by:

ρ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)\displaystyle\rho({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}) =1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|​ψ^†​(𝐫)​ψ^​(𝐫′)​|Ψ⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\langle\Psi|\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\hat{\psi}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})|\Psi\rangle
=1⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩​∑n=0∞n​∫dn−1𝐫​φn∗​(𝐫,𝐫2,…,𝐫N)​φn​(𝐫′,𝐫2,…,𝐫n)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n\int\differential^{n-1}{\mathbf{r}}\varphi_{n}^{*}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{N})\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{n})
=𝔼n∼Pn𝔼𝐫n∼|φ¯n|2[nφn∗​(𝐫n|𝐫1=𝐫)​φn​(𝐫n|𝐫1=𝐫′)∫d​𝐫1​|φn​(𝐫n)|2]\displaystyle=\EX_{n\sim P_{n}}\EX_{{\mathbf{r}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\biggr[n\frac{\varphi_{n}^{*}({\mathbf{r}}_{n}|{\mathbf{r}}_{1}={\mathbf{r}})\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{n}|{\mathbf{r}}_{1}={\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{\int d{\mathbf{r}}_{1}|\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}_{n})|^{2}}\biggr] (81)

A direct evaluation of the above expression involves numerical integration over a 2⋅d2\cdot d-dimensional grid, which becomes computationally challenging for d=2d=2. One possible approach to avoid the direct integration is to employ the so-called natural orbitals, which play a role similar to marginal distributions for probability densities [50]. The idea is based on projecting the OBDM into an orthogonal basis set ϕ1​(𝐫),…,ϕM​(𝐫)\phi_{1}({\mathbf{r}}),...,\phi_{M}({\mathbf{r}}), such that elements of the projected OBDM, ρi​j\rho_{ij}, are given by

ρi​j=∫d​𝐫​d​𝐫′​ϕi​(𝐫)​ϕj​(𝐫′)​ρ​(𝐫,𝐫′)\rho_{ij}=\int d{\mathbf{r}}d{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\rho({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}) (82)

In the case of a single state, a Monte Carlo estimator for ρi​j\rho_{ij} can be written as [50]:

⟨ρ^i​j⟩=𝔼𝐫n∼|φ¯n|2𝔼𝐫′∼ρ[ϕi​(𝐫)​ϕj​(𝐫′)​φn​(𝐫′,𝐫2,…,𝐫n)ρ⁡(𝐫′)​φn​(𝐫,𝐫2,…,𝐫n)]\langle\hat{\rho}_{ij}\rangle=\EX_{{\mathbf{r}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\EX_{{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}\sim\rho}\biggr[\frac{\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{n})}{\rho({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\varphi_{n}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}_{2},...,{\mathbf{r}}_{n})}\biggr] (83)

where ρ\rho is an arbitrary probability distribution over single particle states. While any ρ\rho can work in principle, selecting a distribution that more closely approximates the actual boson density results in an estimator with reduced variance. For instance, in the case of bosons confined in a two-dimensional harmonic potential (see Sec. III.3), an appropriate choice for the orthonormal basis would be the set of eigenfunctions of the corresponding single-particle Hamiltonian and a practical choice for ρ\rho is the ground-state density of a single harmonically trapped boson:

ρ⁡(𝐫)=β2π​e−β2​𝐫2.\rho({\mathbf{r}})=\frac{\beta^{2}}{\pi}e^{-\beta^{2}{\mathbf{r}}^{2}}. (84)

Appendix G Convergence Analysis

The primary observable tracked during the VMC procedure is the total energy that we estimate as empirical means over all collected samples:

E¯=𝔼n∼Pn𝔼𝐑n∼|φ¯n|2​[Enloc​(𝐑n)]≈1Ns​∑i=1NsEnloc​(𝐑n(i))\bar{E}=\EX_{n\sim P_{n}}\EX_{{\mathbf{R}}_{n}\sim|\bar{\varphi}_{n}|^{2}}\left[E^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n})\right]\approx\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}E^{\text{loc}}_{n}({\mathbf{R}}_{n}^{(i)}) (85)

The uncertainty in the estimated expectation value is computed as the standard deviation of the means across the chains (standard error):

Δ​E=1Nc​∑c=1Nc(E¯c−E¯)2\Delta E=\frac{1}{N_{c}}\sqrt{\sum_{c=1}^{N_{c}}\left(\bar{E}_{c}-\bar{E}\right)^{2}} (86)

where NcN_{c} is the number of MCMC chains, and E¯c\bar{E}_{c} is the mean local energy of the cc-th chain.

Additionally, to analyze convergence during optimization and evaluate the resulting performance of the architectures, we introduce the rescaled variance parameter, defined as:

σ~E2=N​⟨H2⟩−⟨H⟩2⟨H⟩2\tilde{\sigma}^{2}_{E}=N\frac{\langle H^{2}\rangle-\langle H\rangle^{2}}{\langle H\rangle^{2}} (87)

This metric is closely related to the V-score, which is defined for spin systems and is known to correlate with the accuracy of the wave function [63]. Like the V-score, the rescaled variance provides a reliable measure of wave function accuracy and can be computed entirely independently of exact reference energies. Figure 8 shows the energy along with the rescaled variance σ~E2\tilde{\sigma}^{2}_{E} during the optimization of the TF ansatz applied to the one-dimensional Calogero-Sutherland model. The plot illustrates how the energy converges to the exact ground-state value, while the rescaled variance simultaneously drops to a value on the order of 10−510^{-5}, confirming a good approximation of the true ground state.

Appendix H Two-dimensional Calogero–Sutherland model

The exact ground state of the Calogero–Sutherland model in arbitrary dimensions was studied in Ref. [31]. Here, we present an overview of the specific two-dimensional case considered in the main text. The ground-state eigenfunction and eigenvalue of the two-dimensional Hamiltonian are given by:

Ψ0=C^exp(−ω2∑i=1Nri2)∏i<j|𝐫i−𝐫j|Λ2,\Psi_{0}=\hat{C}\exp\left(-\frac{\omega}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}r_{i}^{2}\right)\prod_{i<j}|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|^{\Lambda_{2}}, (88)
E0=[2​N+N⁡(N−1)​Λ2]​ω,E_{0}=[2N+N(N-1)\Lambda_{2}]\omega, (89)

where ω\omega denotes the frequency of the harmonic trap, and we have chosen units such that ℏ=2​m=1\hbar=2m=1. The parameter Λ2\Lambda_{2} is defined as:

Λ2=G/2=g/2.\Lambda_{2}=\sqrt{G/2}=\sqrt{g/2}. (90)

By expressing the position vectors 𝐫i∈ℝ2\mathbf{r}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} as complex numbers zi∈ℂz_{i}\in\mathbb{C}, the ground-state probability density can be rewritten as:

|Ψ0|2=Cexp(−Λ2∑i=1N|zi|2)∏i<j|zi−zj|2​Λ2.|\Psi_{0}|^{2}=C\exp\left(-\Lambda_{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|z_{i}|^{2}\right)\prod_{i<j}|z_{i}-z_{j}|^{2\Lambda_{2}}. (91)

For the special case of Λ2=1\Lambda_{2}=1 (which corresponds to g=G=2g=G=2), the density |Ψ0|2|\Psi_{0}|^{2} in Eq. (91) takes the exact form of the joint probability density function for the eigenvalues of matrices drawn from an ensemble of complex random matrices [43]. Following Ref. [43], one can systematically derive the nn-point correlation functions for all nn. In particular, the one-point correlation function, interpreted as the particle number density, is given by:

ℛ⁡(r)=ωπ​Λ2​exp⁡(−ω​r2)​∑p=0N−1(ω​r2)pp!.\mathcal{R}(r)=\frac{\omega}{\pi\Lambda_{2}}\exp(-\omega r^2)\sum_{p=0}^{N-1}\frac{(\omega r^{2})^{p}}{p!}. (92)

As shown in Fig. 5 of the main text, this density profile is completely isotropic and does not depend on the angular coordinate.
